title: Comments, Formatting and Readable C++ Code
learningObjectives: Explain comments, formatting and readable c++ code.
Recognize the relevant C++ syntax and standard-library convention.
Trace examples and predict their output or behaviour.
Use the topic in a small practical program.
Identify a likely mistake and describe how to avoid it.

understand.concept: Comments are notes for human readers and are ignored as program instructions. Consistent formatting, indentation and meaningful names make C++ easier to understand, review and maintain. Formatting does not change the language's meaning, but clarity helps prevent mistakes.
understand.whyItMatters: This concept helps learners write understandable, correct programs and communicate intent to other developers.
understand.analogy: Think of the concept as a clear instruction or label in a workshop that helps everyone use the equipment correctly.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy is a guide only; C++ grammar and execution rules define actual behaviour.
understand.explain:
## Comments
Single-line comments begin with `//`. Block comments use `/* ... */` and can span multiple lines. Comments should explain intent, decisions or constraints rather than restating obvious code.

## Readability
Use meaningful identifiers, consistent indentation, small functions and whitespace to separate ideas. Keep formatting consistent within a project. Avoid misleading comments that become stale.

examples.title: Single-line comment
examples.code: // Convert minutes to seconds\nint seconds = minutes * 60;
examples.explanation: Comments are useful when intent is not obvious.

examples.title: Block comment
examples.code: /* This calculation assumes the input\n   is already validated. */\nint subtotal = 25;
examples.explanation: Block comments can cover multiple lines.

examples.title: Readable names
examples.code: int itemCount = 4;\ndouble unitPrice = 12.5;\ndouble totalCost = itemCount * unitPrice;
examples.explanation: Names communicate meaning better than cryptic abbreviations.

examples.title: Consistent indentation
examples.explanation: Indentation reveals nesting to readers; the braces provide the actual structure.

examples.title: Comment intent
examples.code: // Reject negative quantities before calculating a total\nif (quantity < 0) { /* validation */ }
examples.explanation: Comments should document purpose and constraints, not duplicate the statement.

practise.guidedTask: Run through one example manually, predict what happens, and change one input or statement. Explain the change before testing it.
practise.independentTask: Create a short C++ program that demonstrates this topic in a useful everyday scenario. Include two test cases and verify your expected behaviour.
hints: Read compiler or runtime messages carefully.
Check unusual inputs, not only the happy path.

questions.prompt: Which comment syntax starts a single-line comment?
Which is a valid multi-line comment?
What primarily determines code block structure?
options: Braces and language syntax, not indentation
questions.answer: Braces and language syntax, not indentation
questions.explanation: Indentation aids readers, but braces define blocks.
